Ecumenical

ek-yoo-MEN-ih-kul -- from Greek oikoumene ('the inhabited world') -- not a standalone modern English word. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

To be ecumenical is to be universal in applicability.

The city organized an ecumenical Thanksgiving service, inviting leaders and members from a dozen different religious traditions to take part together.

Worked Example

Rather than favoring one denomination, the charity took an ecumenical approach, welcoming volunteers and donations from every faith community in town.

Ecumenical describes something deliberately open to all groups, especially across religious or denominational lines -- the emphasis is on inclusive cooperation rather than favoring one side.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

interfaith: Interfaith simply states that several different religions are involved -- an interfaith panel has members of many faiths. Ecumenical adds the spirit of the gathering: a deliberate effort to cooperate as equals across religious lines rather than merely sharing a room.

all-embracing: All-embracing means taking in everyone and everything, refusing to leave anyone out, in any setting at all. Ecumenical is the more specific word: deliberate openness across religious groups and denominations in particular, cooperation among faiths rather than general wide-open welcome.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

sectarian: narrowly focused on one group or faction

insular: closed off from outside groups or influences

Where it sits · how widely it reaches across groups — inclusive → ecumenical → universal

inclusive vs. ecumenical: Inclusive means deliberately welcoming a wide range of people or views, and it is a weaker, more general claim than ecumenical, which names active cooperation across entire religious traditions.

universal vs. ecumenical: Universal is the broadest term, applying to absolutely everyone or everything without qualification, even beyond ecumenical's usual religious focus.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — ecumen

Root — ecumen: the inhabited world (from Greek oikoumene -- a word that never became a standalone English word)

Suffix — -ical

Suffix — -ical: having the qualities of; pertaining to

Put it together

Put it together: Ecumen (from Greek oikoumene, 'the inhabited world' -- the whole known world, as the ancient Greeks understood it) + -ical spell ecumenical. Oikoumene never became a common English word on its own, but its idea of 'everyone, everywhere' survives directly in ecumenical.

Where This Word Comes From

Where This Word Comes From: Ecumenical comes from the ancient Greek word oikoumene, meaning 'the inhabited world' -- the whole known world, as the ancient Greeks understood it. That word never became a common English word on its own, but its idea of 'everyone, everywhere' survives directly in ecumenical.

Word Choice

Ecumenical is most often used specifically about religious cooperation across different faiths or denominations, though it can describe any effort to be universally inclusive rather than narrow.
